Hypothesis: Under the A-share no-short-sale regime, the ratio of the 20-day mean to the 120-day mean of daily yuan turnover ($vwap×$volume) measures a surge in opinion divergence and retail attention; since pessimists can only abstain, price is set by optimists and carries a resale-option premium (Miller 1977; Scheinkman-Xiong 2003) that deflates when attention mean-reverts, so HIGH factor values predict LOWER forward returns over the next 10-20 trading days.
                Concise Observation: The scenario covers a retail-dominated A-share market with no practical short selling, annual share turnover in the hundreds of percent, and the 2006-07 bull, 2008 crash and 2009 recovery all inside the window; the daily data provides price, vwap and volume but no float shares, so the 20-day mean yuan turnover must be scaled by each stock's own 120-day mean, otherwise its cross-sectional rank merely restates persistent firm size and liquidity.
                Concise Justification: Without short selling, the marginal buyer of a widely disputed stock is an optimist, so the most churned names trade above any representative valuation (Miller 1977), and high turnover is the footprint of the resale-option component of price that expands with divergence (Scheinkman-Xiong 2003); because retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, the premium decays and the most churned stocks underperform over the next 10-20 trading days.
                Concise Knowledge: If short sales are unavailable so pessimists can only abstain from trading, then abnormal turnover relative to a stock's own baseline proxies the width of opinion divergence and the resale-option premium embedded in price; when attention and divergence mean-revert, the premium deflates, so high abnormal turnover predicts lower returns over the following 10-20 trading days, most strongly in retail-driven bull phases.
                concise Specification: Factor TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120: per stock per day, yuan turnover = $vwap×$volume and F = mean(turnover, past 20 trading days) / mean(turnover, past 120 trading days), set to null when the 120-day history is incomplete; F is cross-sectionally ranked each day and tested against 10-20 day forward returns with a committed negative RankIC over the full window and separately in the 2006-07 bull, 2008 crash and 2009 recovery subsamples, where the effect should be strongest when retail participation peaks.
                Expected IC Sign: negative

factors.name: TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120
factors.description: Implements the Miller (1977) / Scheinkman-Xiong (2003) resale-option premium proxy for the A-share no-short-sale regime. Daily yuan turnover is defined as $vwap x $volume. The factor is the ratio of the 20-day trailing mean to the 120-day trailing mean of turnover, so each stock's short-run turnover surge is scaled by its own long-run baseline; this removes persistent firm size and liquidity differences that would otherwise dominate a raw cross-sectional turnover rank. Because pessimists can only abstain when short selling is unavailable, abnormally high churn marks names whose marginal buyers are optimists and whose prices carry a resale-option premium; as retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, this premium deflates, so HIGH factor values predict LOWER forward returns over the next 10-20 trading days (committed negative RankIC, strongest in retail-driven bull phases). The 120-day rolling mean is undefined (null) until the long history is complete, which automatically nulls the factor for newly listed or insufficient-history stocks.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 120) + 1e-8))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

Observations: This is the first factor admitted to an empty repository (repository size 0), so all comparative dimensions scored the neutral 0.500 baseline; the utility of 0.5458 was pulled above neutral almost entirely by the outstanding overfit-survival score of 0.958 — the in-sample edge genuinely survived out of sample. The pre-registered direction was CONFIRMED: committed negative, measured negative (raw RankIC -0.0170, neutralized -0.0189, Newey-West t = -3.93, exactly clearing the 3.93 multiple-testing bar), with clean decile monotonicity in the predicted direction (-0.71) and a flipped long/short Sharpe of +1.49. Engineering quality is excellent: only 75 symbols (well inside the 50-150 simplicity target), daily one-way turnover of just 0.0431, capacity of 5.1e10 CNY, size correlation of only +0.082, and zero overlap with existing holdings. However, three measurements qualify the victory: (1) the edge is strongest at a 1-DAY horizon, not the hypothesized 10-20 days; (2) stability is weak — RankICIR of -0.146 sits below even the 0.20 'weak' industry bar, with the IC keeping its sign on only 54.6% of days; (3) the edge is regime-concentrated — IC on the worst 20% of cross-sectional days is -0.0758 while on the best 20% it flips to +0.0203. Economically, the factor pays for its own trading 4.5x over (|IC| 0.0189 vs the 0.0042 self-cost bar), but the one-factor book is 5.1x short of net profitability (composite |IC| 0.0170 vs 0.0872 needed) — a book-level property requiring many more independent bets, roughly (0.0872/0.017)^2 ≈ 26 factors of this quality, or fewer but stronger ones.
Hypothesis Evaluation: The core of the hypothesis is SUPPORTED: under the no-short-sale regime, high abnormal turnover (20d/120d surge) marks names whose marginal buyers are optimists, and HIGH values predict LOWER forward returns — the direction, mechanism, and sign all checked out, and the factor cleared admission on its first attempt. But two secondary predictions were REFUTED by the measurement. First, the horizon: the hypothesis said the resale-option premium deflates over 10-20 days as attention mean-reverts 'within weeks'; the measured edge is strongest at 1 day, meaning attention-driven overpricing reverts far faster than the Miller/Scheinkman-Xiong 'weeks' story implies — the 20/120 window pair is likely too slow for where the edge actually lives. Second, the regime: the hypothesis predicted the edge would be 'strongest in retail-driven bull phases'; the measurement shows the opposite — the negative IC is concentrated in the worst 20% of days (-0.0758, four times the overall IC) and flips weakly positive in rallies (+0.0203). The premium deflates hardest when the tape falls (attention collapses in crashes), while in rallies high-churn names keep riding the bubble. The factor is therefore a downside-protection signal: it discriminates well precisely when the book needs it most, but its day-to-day consistency (ICIR -0.146, sign persistence 54.6%) must improve for it to carry a book rather than just hedge one.
New Hypothesis: Refinement within the same Miller (1977) / Scheinkman-Xiong (2003) framework: the resale-option premium attached to abnormal turnover is a FAST-deflating, crash-concentrated phenomenon — attention surges revert within ~1-5 days, and the negative forward-return edge is strongest in falling markets. Therefore shorter, more robust surge measures should raise both the IC magnitude and the day-to-day stability (RankICIR toward the 0.20 bar) relative to the 20/120 pair. Specific variants to test next, each as a separate simple factor (<150 symbols, one window pair per factor): (1) HORIZON MATCHING — shorten the numerator to match the 1-day edge: RANK(TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume, 5) / (TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume, 60) + 1e-8)) and a 10/60 pair; (2) PURE CHURN — isolate attention from price drift by dropping $vwap: RANK(TS_MEAN($volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($volume, 120) + 1e-8)), since yuan turnover mechanically rises with price run-ups and conflates the reversal effect with the attention effect; (3) OUTLIER ROBUSTNESS — turnover is heavily right-skewed, so a few extreme days dominate the 20-day mean and destabilize the daily IC; use a geometric/log ratio RANK(TS_MEAN(LOG($vwap*$volume), 20) - TS_MEAN(LOG($vwap*$volume), 120)) or a median-based surge RANK(TS_MEDIAN($vwap*$volume, 20) / (TS_MEDIAN($vwap*$volume, 120) + 1e-8)); (4) STANDARDIZED SURGE — RANK(TS_ZSCORE($vwap*$volume, 120)), the same self-normalized attention concept in one operator; (5) DISAGREEMENT DISPERSION — within the same opinion-divergence theory, turnover volatility is a disagreement proxy: RANK(TS_STD($vwap*$volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($vwap*$volume, 120) + 1e-8)). Also run a small window-pair grid around the current choice — (5,60), (10,60), (10,120), (20,60), (20,240) — to map parameter sensitivity rather than assume 20/120 is optimal.
Decision: True
Reason: Three measured facts drive the refinement. First, the horizon measurement (strongest at 1 day, not 10-20) says the 20-day numerator averages away the very spike it is meant to capture; a 5- or 10-day numerator should align the signal with the horizon where the edge empirically lives and mechanically increase IC per day. Second, the low RankICIR (-0.146) with 54.6% sign persistence indicates the daily signal is noisy — the right-skew of turnover means single blow-off days dominate the flat 20-day mean and then wash out; log/median/z-score constructions suppress those outliers and should convert the crash-day edge (-0.0758) into a more persistent daily discrimination. Third, the crash-day concentration with a rally-day sign flip means part of the current edge may be a price-reversal artifact of using $vwap in the turnover definition; the volume-only variant tests whether the attention channel (the actual Miller/SX variable) is cleaner. All variants stay strictly inside the same theoretical framework — attention and opinion divergence under no-short-sale — so this is hypothesis refinement, not a direction change. Each proposed factor uses only 2-3 raw features and 2-3 operators, staying far below the complexity thresholds (the current factor's 75 symbols had no overfitting warning, and its 0.958 out-of-sample survival shows simplicity is working). These variants also broaden the operator population beyond the current RANK/TS_MEAN duopoly (LOG, TS_ZSCORE, TS_STD, TS_MEDIAN), which improves repository diversity. Finally, the book-level shortfall (5.1x short of the 0.0872 composite-IC bar) is a property of the book, not this factor: the path forward is to keep stacking low-correlation independent bets within and beyond this family, since each independent factor multiplies book IC by sqrt(N) — at the current per-factor IC, roughly 26 independent factors reach the bar, so both stronger variants AND more distinct families are needed.

                Concise Justification: Expected price impact is a genuine trading cost, so equilibrium requires an illiquidity premium in expected returns (Amihud 2002); with index funds and benchmark huggers crowding into the most liquid constituents, less liquid large caps remain structurally under-owned, so their prices are set by investors demanding compensation, implying high illiquidity precedes higher rather than lower returns.

factors.name: Amihud_Illiq_SizeControlled_60D
factors.description: Size-controlled Amihud illiquidity premium over a 60-day window, matching the 1-3 month holding horizon of the hypothesis. The first leg is the persistent price-impact cost: the 60-day mean of daily |return| per yuan of turnover ($vwap*$volume), ranked cross-sectionally. The second leg adds the cross-sectional rank of 60-day mean yuan turnover, the long-window dollar-volume market-cap proxy named in the hypothesis. Because illiquidity rank and size rank are strongly negatively correlated, their sum cancels the common size component to first order: if illiquidity merely proxies small market cap, the two ranks offset and the factor is cross-sectionally flat, while a genuinely high value marks a stock that is more illiquid than its size predicts -- the less liquid, structurally under-owned large caps that benchmark-hugging index flows skip. Under the Amihud (2002) illiquidity-premium premise the factor should therefore carry positive RankIC against forward next-several-day to 3-month returns, and it directly implements the hypothesis's own falsification test (premium must survive a size control).

factors.name: REV5_RANK
factors.description: Short-term reversal factor: cross-sectional percentile rank of the trailing 5-trading-day compounded return. For each instrument on day t, the 5-day cumulative return R5 is computed as the compounded product of (1 + daily return) over the last 5 daily bars minus 1, then percentile-ranked within the cross-section on that date into [0,1], so a higher rank means a larger past 5-day gain. Observations: REV5_RANK = RANK(PROD(1+$return,5)-1) is the cleanest statistical confirmation in this run, and it was KEPT. Pre-registered direction (negative) matches the measured direction and the mechanism was explicitly confirmed. Raw RankIC -0.0656 vs neutralized -0.0585 (small gap, plus SIZE correlation only +0.035, so the edge is alpha rather than repackaged risk exposure); Newey-West t = -10.80 against a 2.87 multiple-testing bar (~3.8x clearance); ICIR -0.401 sits inside the 0.30-0.50 'good' band; decile monotonicity -0.90 is a clean full gradient, not a tails-only signal; sign persistence 66.5%; and the edge is regime-uniform (IC -0.0479 on the worst 20% of cross-section days vs -0.0646 on the best 20%). Standalone economics clear comfortably: |IC| 0.0585 vs 0.0194 needed to pay for its own turnover (3.0x), turnover 0.201/day, capacity 1.09e10 CNY. Dimension scores: stability 1.000, decay 1.000, overfit 0.983 (the in-sample edge survived out-of-sample; complexity is only 30 symbols, far below the 150-character overfitting threshold, so no complexity warning applies), effectiveness/arr/turnover 0.500, diversity 0.000 (worst dimension). Two caveats: (1) the edge is strongest at a 1-DAY forward horizon, not the 5-10 days the hypothesis stated - the reversal is front-loaded and decays fast; (2) the combined book is still 1.3x SHORT of net profitability (composite |IC| 0.0656 vs 0.0872 oracle bar), and since book IC scales with the square root of the number of independent bets, roughly three factors of this quality are needed to clear the book-level bar. The 0.000 diversity score despite a max pairwise correlation of only 0.056 and a marginal effective rank of 1.00 likely reflects population-level construction convergence (RANK appears in 75% of mined factors, only 5/56 operators exercised) rather than pairwise redundancy - the system is asking for a broader toolkit, not for a different signal.
Hypothesis Evaluation: The hypothesis is SUPPORTED in its pre-registered direction: a high cross-sectional rank of the trailing 5-day return predicts lower forward returns, with a monotonic decile gradient and regime-robust IC - exactly what the liquidity-provision/overreaction mechanism predicts. Refine rather than redirect. First, the horizon: the edge peaks at 1 day, so the 'next 5-10 trading days' clause was too slow; bid-ask bounce and the fastest overreaction decay inside 1-3 days. The lookback should be aligned with this fast decay - test 1/3/10/20-day lookbacks as separate static factors, and consider recency-weighted lookbacks (WMA/DECAYLINEAR of daily returns) that tilt toward the most recent day where the edge is strongest. Second, the hypothesis names two distinct drivers - retail chasing and bid-ask bounce - but the current factor cannot separate them; conditioning the 5-day reversal on abnormal volume isolates the chasing channel, and volatility-scaling (dividing the 5-day return by its trailing std) or vwap-based returns reduce microstructure-noise contamination, which should raise ICIR further. Third, turnover: a 1-day-horizon edge degrades fastest under cost; the current 0.201/day is affordable (3.0x its own cost bar), but a smoothed variant (e.g., DECAYLINEAR of the rank over 3 days) is worth testing as a cheaper hold. Finally, address the 0.000 diversity score by varying the construction toolkit (TS_ZSCORE, TS_STD, WMA, DELAY, TS_PCTCHANGE, TS_RANK) instead of adding a fourth RANK-of-price-return factor - keep every new expression short (target 50-150 characters, at most 2-3 raw features), because the current factor's simplicity is a large part of why the overfit score is 0.983.
New Hypothesis: Within the same reversal framework, the reversible component of the past 5-day return is (i) front-loaded in time and (ii) concentrated where abnormal volume marks retail chasing. Three concrete, individually testable refinements, all keeping the negative pre-registered direction and all far below the complexity ceiling: (a) recency-weighted reversal RANK(WMA($return,5)) should beat the equal-weighted 5-day rank because the measured edge peaks at the 1-day horizon; (b) volatility-scaled reversal RANK((PROD(1+$return,5)-1)/(TS_STD($return,20)+1e-8)) should be more stable (higher |ICIR|) because it measures overreaction in units of each name's own noise, directly targeting the bid-ask-bounce component named in the mechanism; (c) volume-conditioned reversal RANK((PROD(1+$return,5)-1)*TS_ZSCORE($volume,20)) should show a stronger negative IC than the unconditional rank if chasing-driven overreaction is the true driver. In parallel, because the book is 1.3x short of net profitability while this factor is uncorrelated with holdings (rho_max 0.056, marginal effective rank 1.00), future rounds should also add low-correlation non-reversal factors (liquidity, volatility, volume-based) so the composite IC scales past the 0.0872 book bar.
Decision: True
Reason: The measurement confirmed both the sign and the stated mechanism with t = -10.80 and ICIR -0.401, so the theoretical framework should be iterated on, not abandoned. The single strongest clue in the data is the horizon: the edge peaks at 1 day, meaning the reversible overreaction is front-loaded - recency weighting (a) exploits this directly and is a one-line change. Volatility scaling (b) follows from the noise/bounce part of the stated mechanism: a raw 5-day return conflates genuine drift with noise-driven moves, and standardizing by trailing return std isolates the standardized 'surprise', which typically improves stability and regime-uniformity (the current ICIR of 0.401 is good but not exhausted). Volume conditioning (c) is the direct test of the retail-chasing channel the hypothesis commits to: if chasing is the driver, the reversal should be stronger where volume is abnormal, and confirming or refuting this sharpens the mechanism itself. All three variants use currently-unused operators (WMA, TS_STD, TS_ZSCORE), which simultaneously attacks the 0.000 diversity score and the population's operator convergence (RANK at 75%), while each expression stays under ~60 characters with at most 2 raw features - preserving the simplicity that gave this factor its 0.983 overfit score. The book-level arithmetic motivates the parallel direction: composite IC scales with sqrt of independent bets, so the 0.0872 bar needs about three uncorrelated factors of this 0.0585 quality; cloning reversal at nearby lookbacks would raise pairwise correlation without adding independent directions, whereas liquidity/volatility/volume families would.

factors.name: Intraday_Minus_Overnight_Return_Spread_20D
factors.description: Cross-sectional rank of the 20-day mean spread between intraday session returns and overnight gap returns, per the target hypothesis. The intraday leg ($close/$open - 1) measures returns earned during the continuous session, interpreted as renewable informed accumulation; the overnight leg ($open/DELAY($close,1) - 1) measures the call-auction gap, interpreted as attention-driven chasing by retail buyers who are locked in under T+1 and become next-session marginal sellers. Because the market's reversal tendency should concentrate on overnight-heavy names, a persistently positive intraday-minus-overnight spread predicts HIGHER forward 10-20 day close-to-close returns (expected positive IC). The spread is averaged over a 20-day window requiring at least 20 valid daily observations, then ranked cross-sectionally. Denominators are guarded with a 1e-8 constant to avoid inf/NaN from zero prices. Diagnostic commitment: the factor must survive size/industry/beta neutralization with a positive sign (unlike the gap level, which was raw-only); if the neutralized IC is <= 0, or overnight and intraday components reverse symmetrically so the spread adds nothing beyond total momentum, the participant-asymmetry premise is falsified and the direction should be abandoned rather than sign-flipped.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN(($close/($open + 1e-8) - 1) - ($open/(DELAY($close, 1) + 1e-8) - 1), 20))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "Intraday_Minus_Overnight_Return_Spread_20D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

factors.name: EXTREME_GAIN_RATIO_20D
factors.description: Scale-free lottery-demand marker for a retail-dominated, no-shorting, limit-board market: daily gains that are extreme relative to the stock's own typical move mark overpricing that unwinds over the next 1-20 days. Numerator: the 75th percentile of daily returns over the past 20 sessions (q = 1 - 5/20 = 0.75), i.e. approximately the 5th-largest daily return, a robust lower-bound proxy for the mean of the 5 largest returns that is exact when extreme gains cluster at the limit-up cap (limit-up streaks). Denominator: the mean absolute daily return over the 60 sessions ending 20 days back (the pre-event typical move), delayed so the event window cannot contaminate its own baseline. The ratio expresses the recent jump in multiples of the stock's own typical daily move, de-conflating limit-up truncation: a limit-up streak in a formerly sleepy name scores far higher than the same streak in a chronically volatile name. Because skewness-preferring retail overweights such lottery jumps and no short sellers compete the overpricing away, HIGH values predict LOWER forward returns (negative IC), most strongly in high-turnover names and speculative episodes. Hyperparameters: event window 20 days, top-k 5 (quantile 0.75), baseline window 60 days delayed 20 days, epsilon 1e-8, daily cross-sectional z-score, evaluation horizons 1/5/20 days.

factors.name: Proximity_to_52W_High_250D
factors.description: Direct implementation of the George-Hwang (2004) 52-week-high anchoring hypothesis: cross-sectional rank of today's close divided by the highest close over the past 250 trading days (52 weeks). A value at or near 1 means price sits at or has just broken its historical peak, exhausting the anchored-supply overhang from holders who bought near the old peak, so net buying meets little resistance and continuation drift follows over the next 5-20 days; stocks far below the anchor face anchored sellers on every approach. The factor is pure anchor proximity with no momentum, liquidity, or volatility terms and no gating, so any incremental payoff versus the book's admitted 5-day momentum, 20/120 liquidity-trend, and return-quantile directions isolates the anchoring mechanism rather than underreaction. The 250-day lookback is mechanically distinct from every short-window direction already in the book, and the full-window requirement leaves new listings as NaN.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(DECAYLINEAR(TS_RANK(TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 120) + 1e-8), 60), 10))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "SUSTAINED_TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

factors.description: Refinement of the admitted parent REV5_RANK = RANK(PROD(1+$return,5)-1). The parent's core construction is kept verbatim as the inner term; the single added modification targets the two lowest-scored dimensions named in the directive (net-of-cost return e=0.50 and in-book diversity e=0.00): a 5-trading-day time-series average of the daily cross-sectional percentile rank of the trailing 5-day compounded return. Averaging the rank over days t-4..t isolates the persistent-winner / persistent-loser component of the 5-day reversal, so (i) the parent's 0.90 turnover share falls sharply because the smoothed rank changes slowly, letting the 0.3-0.6 percent round-trip cost amortize over the 5-10 day holding horizon the specification commits to; (ii) predictive mass shifts away from the untradeable 1-day bounce toward the 5-10 day overreaction-decay horizon where the edge is monetizable; (iii) the slow persistent leg is functionally distinct from the already-held fast short-horizon retail-flow legs, raising marginal in-book value instead of duplicating them; (iv) single-day bid-ask bounce noise that concentrates the raw rank's gross IC at the 1-day horizon is averaged out, reducing the microstructure dependence behind the elevated overfit-risk reading. Direction is preserved: a HIGH value means the instrument was a cross-sectional winner over the recent 5-day windows, predicting LOWER forward 5-10 day returns (negative expected IC). Hyperparameters: return-compounding lookback = 5 trading days (parent's, unchanged), rank-smoothing window = 5 trading days (the single added free parameter); static windows, no thresholds, no coefficients.

factors.name: AMIHUD_IMPACT_SURGE_20_120
factors.description: Episodic price-impact surge factor for the A-share no-short-sale, T+1, retail-dominated regime. Each day it forms the epsilon-guarded Amihud impact I_t = |return| / (vwap*volume + 1e-8), i.e. price move per yuan traded, averages it over the past 20 trading days, and normalizes by the same stock's own 120-day baseline mean before taking the daily cross-sectional percentile rank. The self-baseline normalization strips the persistent, size-dominated level of illiquidity (the failure mode of the level-based parent) and isolates the episodic liquidity-contraction state: a high rank marks an abnormal impact surge, which under short-sale constraints reflects an uncleared one-sided selling overhang hitting a thinned order book (pessimists can only abstain, so supply keeps clearing at lower prices) and a divergence/attention episode whose optimist-set price carries a resale-option premium that deflates as the episode mean-reverts. Expected RankIC sign is negative, strongest at the 1-day horizon and decaying over 5-20 days. Implementation notes: rolling windows 20 (short) and 120 (long baseline) applied per instrument with effective min_periods 15/60; the 1e-8 guards bound zero-dollar-volume days (they contribute ~0 impact when the return is zero) and prevent division blow-ups; output is one static daily cross-sectional percentile rank per instrument.

hypothesis_template.concise_observation: The scenario covers a retail-dominated A-share market with no practical short selling, annual share turnover in the hundreds of percent, and the 2006-07 bull, 2008 crash and 2009 recovery all inside the window; the daily data provides price, vwap and volume but no float shares, so the 20-day mean yuan turnover must be scaled by each stock's own 120-day mean, otherwise its cross-sectional rank merely restates persistent firm size and liquidity.
hypothesis_template.concise_justification: Without short selling, the marginal buyer of a widely disputed stock is an optimist, so the most churned names trade above any representative valuation (Miller 1977), and high turnover is the footprint of the resale-option component of price that expands with divergence (Scheinkman-Xiong 2003); because retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, the premium decays and the most churned stocks underperform over the next 10-20 trading days.
hypothesis_template.concise_knowledge: If short sales are unavailable so pessimists can only abstain from trading, then abnormal turnover relative to a stock's own baseline proxies the width of opinion divergence and the resale-option premium embedded in price; when attention and divergence mean-revert, the premium deflates, so high abnormal turnover predicts lower returns over the following 10-20 trading days, most strongly in retail-driven bull phases.

parent_factors.description: Implements the Miller (1977) / Scheinkman-Xiong (2003) resale-option premium proxy for the A-share no-short-sale regime. Daily yuan turnover is defined as $vwap x $volume. The factor is the ratio of the 20-day trailing mean to the 120-day trailing mean of turnover, so each stock's short-run turnover surge is scaled by its own long-run baseline; this removes persistent firm size and liquidity differences that would otherwise dominate a raw cross-sectional turnover rank. Because pessimists can only abstain when short selling is unavailable, abnormally high churn marks names whose marginal buyers are optimists and whose prices carry a resale-option premium; as retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, this premium deflates, so HIGH factor values predict LOWER forward returns over the next 10-20 trading days (committed negative RankIC, strongest in retail-driven bull phases). The 120-day rolling mean is undefined (null) until the long history is complete, which automatically nulls the factor for newly listed or insufficient-history stocks.

factors.description: Band-consumption rank smoothed over 60 trading days. Each day's band consumption is the signed daily return scaled by the instrument's exchange daily price band and clipped to the full-limit range [-1, 1]. A HIGH value marks an instrument whose advances repeatedly consumed most of their daily band over the window — attention-driven retail marketable-order pushes past where informed flow clears, accumulated under the band and T+1 rule — so HIGH values predict LOWER forward 1/5/20-day returns (committed negative size/industry/beta-neutralized RankIC). import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "TS_MEAN(RANK(MIN(MAX($return / (MIN(MAX(TS_MAX(ABS($return), 250), 0.1), 0.21) + 1e-8), -1), 1)) - 0.5, 60)" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "BANDCONS_RANK_60D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

The hypothesis is that retail marketable order flow chases recent moves and pushes high-rank names past the level where informed flow would clear, so liquidity suppliers earn the bounce back as overreaction and bid-ask bounce decay over the next 5-10 trading days; hence the ranked past 5-day return should carry negative information about forward returns at that horizon.

factors.description: Persistent lottery-fame factor on the skip-month window. Core: the daily cross-sectional z-score of the 90th percentile of daily returns over t-252..t-21, implemented as a 231-day rolling quantile of the 21-day-delayed return (the single 90th percentile is the compact equivalent of the mean of the 75th and 95th percentiles, whose average sits near the 87th-90th percentile for near-Gaussian upper tails). Each day the core is residualized by an exact cross-sectional OLS against the z-scored same-window limit-up-day count (delayed daily return > 9.5%) -- the limit-up cleaning repair validated in the short-horizon parent, lifted to the annual horizon -- and netted against the z-scored log 231-day mean dollar-volume size proxy with a unit standardized loading; since the scoring pipeline neutralizes size/beta/industry, the unit loading leaves the neutralized content identical to exact OLS size removal while guaranteeing the mandated in-factor size scrub. The residual is then smoothed with a 5-day trailing mean and re-standardized daily. Mechanism: year-long salience sustains retail lottery demand that keeps such names overpriced in the absence of short sellers, so HIGH factor values predict LOWER forward returns (expected IC sign negative at 1/5/20-day horizons). Budget-driven deviations from the full specification, forced by the 250-character expression limit: the recent 20-day tail-quantile control is omitted (a unit-loading subtraction of that positively lottery-loaded control would invert the factor's lottery loading, and the delay-21 skip-month window already limits overlap with the short-horizon lottery core), and the 75th/95th-percentile pair is proxied by the single 90th percentile.

The 5-over-60 self-normalization strips out the persistent cross-sectional illiquidity level that proxied size (the parent's SIZE correlation +0.1854) and mechanically decorrelates the factor from the library's return-per-yuan-volume level factor, isolating the innovation: a spike in price impact per yuan of turnover relative to a stock's own norm marks a transient liquidity-demand shock from impatient flow that pushes the price away from value. Once that impatient flow passes, the price mean-reverts, so a HIGH factor value predicts LOWER forward returns over the next 1-5 days (negative expected RankIC, strongest at the 1-day horizon, persisting through 5 days and fading by 20).

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN(ABS($return)/($vwap*$volume+1e-8),5) / (TS_MEAN(ABS($return)/($vwap*$volume+1e-8),60)+1e-14))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "ILLIQ_SHOCK_5_60" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

parent_factors.description: Net count of near-limit-up closes minus near-limit-down closes over the past 60 trading days, implementing the band-truncation demand-carryover hypothesis on the SH/SZ daily panel. Since instrument codes are not available inside the expression, the two regime bands are covered by disjoint close-to-close return windows: a daily return in [9.5%, 11.0%] flags a close at or within 0.5pp of the 10% main-board band, and a return in [19.5%, 21.0%] flags the 20% band of STAR names and post-2020-08-24 ChiNext names; the +1pp upper slack keeps no-band sessions such as IPO debuts out of the count. Symmetric windows around -10% and -20% define near-limit-down events. A high net count indicates repeated one-sided demand truncated by the daily band, with unfilled limit orders queuing into subsequent sessions while the T+1 rule delays profit-taking, so the factor is committed to a positive cross-sectional RankIC against 1-5 day forward returns. Raw integer count, no normalization; undefined until 60 observations exist.

The intraday leg ($close/$open - 1) measures returns earned during the continuous session, interpreted as renewable informed accumulation; the overnight leg ($open/DELAY($close,1) - 1) measures the call-auction gap, interpreted as attention-driven chasing by retail buyers who are locked in under T+1 and become next-session marginal sellers. import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN(($close/($open + 1e-8) - 1) - ($open/(DELAY($close, 1) + 1e-8) - 1), 20))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "Intraday_Minus_Overnight_Return_Spread_20D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

parent_factors.description: Scale-free lottery-demand marker for a retail-dominated, no-shorting, limit-board market: daily gains that are extreme relative to the stock's own typical move mark overpricing that unwinds over the next 1-20 days. Numerator: the 75th percentile of daily returns over the past 20 sessions (q = 1 - 5/20 = 0.75), i.e. approximately the 5th-largest daily return, a robust lower-bound proxy for the mean of the 5 largest returns that is exact when extreme gains cluster at the limit-up cap (limit-up streaks). Denominator: the mean absolute daily return over the 60 sessions ending 20 days back (the pre-event typical move), delayed so the event window cannot contaminate its own baseline. The ratio expresses the recent jump in multiples of the stock's own typical daily move, de-conflating limit-up truncation: a limit-up streak in a formerly sleepy name scores far higher than the same streak in a chronically volatile name. Because skewness-preferring retail overweights such lottery jumps and no short sellers compete the overpricing away, HIGH values predict LOWER forward returns (negative IC), most strongly in high-turnover names and speculative episodes. Hyperparameters: event window 20 days, top-k 5 (quantile 0.75), baseline window 60 days delayed 20 days, epsilon 1e-8, daily cross-sectional z-score, evaluation horizons 1/5/20 days.

Each day the name's proximity to its long-horizon price anchor is measured as the adjusted close divided by the trailing 250-day maximum close; this raw level is then self-normalized against the name's own trailing 60-day history with a time-series rank (stripping the size/level exposure that carried the raw anchor level's positive raw IC), and the resulting self-rank is smoothed with a 10-day linear decay so that only names whose anchor proximity has been persistently elevated for roughly the past two weeks score high. The cross-sectional rank of that sustained anchor extension is expected to carry a NEGATIVE RankIC against 1-10 day forward returns after size/industry neutralization: with short sales barred, a name held persistently at its most salient long-horizon anchor is priced by the optimist set and carries a resale-option premium (Miller 1977; Scheinkman-Xiong 2003) that deflates when attention mean-reverts. Static hyperparameters: anchor window 250 trading days, self-rank window 60 days, linear-decay window 10 days, denominator guard 1e-8; the factor is null for the first 250 days of each name's history and is computed daily per instrument on adjusted close.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(DECAYLINEAR(TS_RANK($close/(TS_MAX($close,250)+1e-8),60),10))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "SUSTAINED_ANCHOR_EXTENSION_250_60_10" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

hypothesis_template.hypothesis: Proximity to the trailing 52-week high — today's adjusted close divided by the highest adjusted close over the past 250 trading days, evaluated as a cross-sectional rank — predicts HIGHER forward returns: a HIGH proximity value (price at or near its 52-week high) forecasts HIGHER returns over the next 5-20 trading days, strongest at the 20-day horizon, because breaking the historical peak exhausts the supply overhang from holders anchored to that peak and the drift continues, whereas stocks far below the anchor meet anchored supply on every approach; the effect must survive incremental to raw momentum, since anchoring (George-Hwang 2004) rather than underreaction is the operative mechanism.
hypothesis_template.concise_observation: After the 2008 crash most of this cross-section trades far below its 52-week high, so the proximity ratio enters 2009 with unusually wide dispersion; the admitted book already monetizes short-horizon reversal (5-day momentum held with a negative weight) plus a 20/120-day liquidity trend and a return-quantile direction (combined rank IC +0.0231), 10 of 14 rejected factors realized negative IC, and the rejected seller-exhaustion factor paid only on market-stress days (ic_crash +0.034 vs ic_rally -0.022, best horizon 1 day) — leaving long-window anchor continuation as an unclaimed direction mechanically distinct from the book.
hypothesis_template.concise_justification: Holders who bought near the old peak anchor to it and sell into subsequent approaches, capping price below fundamental value; once price breaks the peak the overhang above is exhausted, so returning buy flow meets little resistance and continuation follows (George-Hwang 2004); because the driver is anchored supply rather than slow information diffusion, proximity should forecast returns incremental to raw momentum, and by the mirror image of the measured exhaustion payoff it should concentrate on non-stress days.
hypothesis_template.concise_knowledge: If traders anchor to a salient historical price peak, a stock's proximity to that peak forecasts returns beyond its recent trend: when price approaches the 52-week high from below, holders who bought near the old peak supply into the approach and hold price below fundamentals; when the peak finally breaks, no anchored seller remains above and small net buying produces continuation drift; if a market instead mean-reverts at every horizon, anchor proximity adds nothing beyond short-window reversal and the anchoring premise is false.

parent_factors.name: Proximity_to_52W_High_250D
parent_factors.description: Direct implementation of the George-Hwang (2004) 52-week-high anchoring hypothesis: cross-sectional rank of today's close divided by the highest close over the past 250 trading days (52 weeks). A value at or near 1 means price sits at or has just broken its historical peak, exhausting the anchored-supply overhang from holders who bought near the old peak, so net buying meets little resistance and continuation drift follows over the next 5-20 days; stocks far below the anchor face anchored sellers on every approach. The factor is pure anchor proximity with no momentum, liquidity, or volatility terms and no gating, so any incremental payoff versus the book's admitted 5-day momentum, 20/120 liquidity-trend, and return-quantile directions isolates the anchoring mechanism rather than underreaction. The 250-day lookback is mechanically distinct from every short-window direction already in the book, and the full-window requirement leaves new listings as NaN.

                Concise Observation: The scenario covers a retail-dominated A-share market with no practical short selling, annual share turnover in the hundreds of percent, and the 2006-07 bull, 2008 crash and 2009 recovery all inside the window; the daily data provides price, vwap and volume but no float shares, so the 20-day mean yuan turnover must be scaled by each stock's own 120-day mean, otherwise its cross-sectional rank merely restates persistent firm size and liquidity.
                Concise Justification: Without short selling, the marginal buyer of a widely disputed stock is an optimist, so the most churned names trade above any representative valuation (Miller 1977), and high turnover is the footprint of the resale-option component of price that expands with divergence (Scheinkman-Xiong 2003); because retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, the premium decays and the most churned stocks underperform over the next 10-20 trading days.
                Concise Knowledge: If short sales are unavailable so pessimists can only abstain from trading, then abnormal turnover relative to a stock's own baseline proxies the width of opinion divergence and the resale-option premium embedded in price; when attention and divergence mean-revert, the premium deflates, so high abnormal turnover predicts lower returns over the following 10-20 trading days, most strongly in retail-driven bull phases.
                concise Specification: Factor TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120: per stock per day, yuan turnover = $vwap×$volume and F = mean(turnover, past 20 trading days) / mean(turnover, past 120 trading days), set to null when the 120-day history is incomplete; F is cross-sectionally ranked each day and tested against 10-20 day forward returns with a committed negative RankIC over the full window and separately in the 2006-07 bull, 2008 crash and 2009 recovery subsamples, where the effect should be strongest when retail participation peaks.

factors.name: REV5_OWNBASE120_SMOOTH5
factors.description: Self-baseline-normalized short-horizon reversal. The stock's 5-day compounded return is divided by its own 120-day mean absolute 5-day move, isolating the overextension component of the move relative to the stock's own typical swing: moves within the stock's own norm are routine volatility pricing with little reversion, while own-norm excess marks retail-chasing beyond where informed flow clears and is precisely the component that mean-reverts. Dividing out the own-volatility baseline strips the size/volatility common exposure that makes raw reversal ranks redundant with the held library (targeting rho_max<0.6 versus the parents' 0.67/0.64). The ratio is taken as a daily cross-sectional percentile rank and the rank is smoothed over 5 days for steadiness, inheriting from the reversal parent its validated quantity, negative direction and rank-smoothing, and from the impact parent its own-baseline normalization with epsilon guard and 1-day horizon concentration, while deliberately excluding the Amihud impact term whose unconfirmed positive sign could fight the validated negative one. Hyperparameters fixed: 5-day return window, 120-day own-baseline window, 5-day rank-smoothing window, epsilon 1e-8 (requires about 124 trading days of history). Expected sign: negative - a HIGH factor value predicts LOWER forward returns over the next 1-5 trading days, strongest at the 1-day horizon.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "TS_MEAN(RANK((PROD(1+$return,5)-1)/(TS_MEAN(ABS(PROD(1+$return,5)-1),120)+1e-8)),5)" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "REV5_OWNBASE120_SMOOTH5" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

bc65c45c3cb3.feedback:
Observations: REV5_OWNBASE120_SMOOTH5 is the statistically strongest reversal variant tested so far, and the hypothesis was confirmed on every pre-registered prediction: direction negative (neutralized RankIC -0.0422, t -8.54, clearing both the incumbent's |t| of 6.72 and the multiple-testing bar of 1.71), horizon strongest at 1 day exactly as committed, sign persistence 63.4% of days, ICIR -0.317 (above the 0.30 'good' bar), decile monotonicity -0.78 (a clean gradient, not tails-only), and the mechanism explicitly confirmed by the evaluator. Crucially, raw IC (-0.0412) is nearly identical to neutralized IC (-0.0422) with size correlation only +0.033, so the own-baseline division did strip the size/volatility common exposure and what remains is alpha, not repackaged risk. The edge is regime-robust (IC negative on both worst-20% days at -0.0504 and best-20% days at -0.0294, actually stronger in down markets). Economics are healthy at the factor level: turnover 0.1347 one-way daily, |IC| 3.2x the own-turnover breakeven (0.0422 vs 0.0130), capacity 1.63e10 CNY, complexity 83 symbols (no overfit flag; overfit and stability scores both 1.000, decay 0.800). THE FAILURE IS DIVERSITY, scored 0.000: max correlation with the held library is 0.851 per-factor (0.950 at book level) versus the explicitly stated target of rho_max<0.6, i.e. WORSE than the parents' 0.67/0.64. Dividing by a slow 120-day per-stock scalar perturbs the cross-sectional ordering too little, and the shared skeleton RANK + TS_MEAN(.,5) locks in the parent TS_MEAN(RANK(PROD(1+$return,5)-1),5). Consequently the round utility is only 0.58, dragged down entirely by the redundancy, and the book remains 2.1x SHORT of net profitability (book |IC| 0.0412 vs 0.0872 needed), because a redundant bet cannot raise the book IC, which scales with the square root of the number of INDEPENDENT bets (the book needs roughly 4x more independent signals).
Hypothesis Evaluation: The hypothesis is SUPPORTED on mechanism and direction, and REFUTED on its decorrelation claim. The core theoretical claim - that the component of a 5-day move in excess of the stock's own typical swing is what mean-reverts, while within-norm moves are routine volatility pricing - is validated: normalizing by the own baseline upgraded the parent from |t| 6.72 to 8.54, improved ICIR to 0.317, produced a clean decile gradient, and reduced size exposure to a negligible +0.033. However, the hypothesis explicitly targeted rho_max<0.6 versus the held library and delivered 0.851, a worse redundancy than the parents it was meant to fix. The diagnosis: a cross-sectional RANK of R5 divided by a slowly-varying 120-day scalar is still dominated by the peer-comparison component of RANK - the rank reshuffles only marginally, and the inherited 5-day rank smoothing (identical to the parent's) preserves the parent's time structure. The factor is therefore a better version of the SAME bet, not a new bet. By the repository's own near-duplicate rule it takes the parent's slot (8.54 > 6.72), which is a strict upgrade of that slot, but it adds nothing to the book's independent bet count, which is the binding constraint given the 2.1x shortfall.
New Hypothesis: The mean-reverting component of a short-horizon move is the stock's OWN-HISTORY unusualness rather than its peer-relative size; replacing the weak scalar normalization with a full time-series normalization of the 5-day move within its own 120-day history - e.g. F = TS_MEAN(RANK(TS_ZSCORE(PROD(1+$return,5)-1, 120)), 5), where TS_ZSCORE removes each stock's own drift and scales by its own 5-day-return dispersion - retains the confirmed negative 1-day reversion edge while structurally decorrelating from the cross-sectional reversal family (target rho_max<0.6), because a stock's position within its own history is driven by idiosyncratic unusualness rather than by where the whole cross-section sits today. Secondary variations within the same framework, in order of priority: (1) the purest own-norm implementation F = TS_MEAN(RANK(TS_RANK(PROD(1+$return,5)-1, 120)), 5), where TS_RANK is the move's percentile within its own past 120 days - the most literal reading of 'unusually large relative to the stock's own typical swing'; (2) an asymmetric upside-only variant using MAX(PROD(1+$return,5)-1, 0) in the numerator, isolating the retail-chasing leg the narrative actually describes; (3) dropping or shortening the 5-day rank smoothing (a structural component shared with the parent and thus a correlation driver), accepting somewhat higher turnover given the 3.2x cushion over the own-turnover breakeven. Keep hyperparameters minimal: 5-day return window, 120-day own-history window, optional 5-day smoothing; both proposed forms are ~50-55 symbols, one raw feature ($return), two window parameters.
Decision: True
Reason: Three facts drive the next step. First, the own-norm concept is validated and improved the parent on every statistical dimension, so the theoretical framework should be kept and re-expressed, not abandoned. Second, the 0.851 correlation proves the implementation - not the concept - is redundant: cross-sectional RANK of a slowly-normalized quantity inherits the parent's ordering, so decorrelation requires changing the information source itself, from 'big versus peers today' to 'big versus this stock's own history'. Time-series normalization (TS_ZSCORE or TS_RANK) is exactly that change, is more faithful to the stated mechanism, and uses operators from the 38 still unexercised (TS_ZSCORE, TS_RANK), which also addresses the flagged population convergence on RANK/TS_MEAN/ABS (44% of all calls). Third, the book's 2.1x shortfall means every future factor must clear rho_max<0.6 or it cannot help the book clear its economic bar; the proposed variants are all under 60 symbols, use one raw feature and at most two free parameters, well inside every complexity guard, and preserve the validated rank-and-smooth wrapper and negative 1-day direction. If the TS_ZSCORE variant still correlates above 0.6 with the held library, escalate to the TS_RANK variant, then to removing the shared smoother, before concluding the reversal family is exhausted.

hypothesis_template.hypothesis:
Hypothesis: A HIGH cross-sectionally ranked past 5-trading-day return predicts LOWER forward returns over the next 5-10 trading days in this A-share sample, because retail marketable orders chase recent moves and push prices past where informed flow would clear, so liquidity suppliers earn the bounce back as overreaction and bid-ask bounce decay within days.
                Concise Observation: On this SH/SZ daily-bar book (per-day open, close, high, low, volume, vwap, return per instrument) only three factors have been scored: two were rejected with small negative marginal RankIC (a 60-day Amihud-style illiquidity rank at -0.0152 and a near-limit-up-day counter at -0.0171) and one of the three missed |t|=3 on neutralized correlation, while a dollar-volume ratio factor is the best incumbent (U=0.5458); the negative signs lean the same way as short-term winner reversal, yet no direct past-return factor has been measured yet.
                Concise Justification: In a retail-dominated A-share market, marketable orders chasing recent gains push prices past the level where informed flow would clear, and the supplier of immediacy earns the bounce back as overreaction and bid-ask bounce decay within days; short-horizon contrarian profits documented for the A-share market through the 2000s (e.g., Kang-Liu-Ni 2002) support the commitment that a high past 5-day return predicts lower next-5-10-day returns.
                Concise Knowledge: If a market's short-horizon order flow is dominated by retail marketable orders that chase recent moves, past 5-day returns reverse over the following 5-10 days and the cross-sectionally ranked past 5-day return carries negative information about forward returns; when part of the bounce-back is bid-ask microstructure noise, the tradeable edge concentrates at the 5-10 day horizon net of roughly 0.3-0.6 percent round-trip cost rather than at the 1-day horizon where the bounce is too small to trade.
                concise Specification: Factor REV5_RANK: on each day t for each instrument compute the trailing 5-trading-day cumulative return R5 as the compounded product of (1 + daily $return) over the last 5 daily bars minus 1 (equivalently adjusted close at t divided by adjusted close at t-5 minus 1), then cross-sectionally percentile-rank R5 within each datetime into [0, 1] so a higher rank means a larger past 5-day gain; source data is daily_pv.h5, lookback window = 5 trading days, single static window, no smoothing; commitment: negative cross-sectional RankIC of REV5_RANK against forward returns over the next 5-10 trading days, evaluated net of roughly 0.3-0.6 percent round-trip cost, with the 5-10 day horizon preferred over the 1-day horizon.
                Expected IC Sign: negative

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe

    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)

parent_factors.description: Crossover child realizing the hypothesis: the adjusted price level attribute from Parent 2 (LOG($close+1e-8), re-confirmed +0.0201 rank IC, positive direction, slow decay) repaired by Parent 1's measured liquidity-group demeaning. Daily dollar volume dv=$vwap*$volume is smoothed per instrument over a trailing 63-day window (TS_MEAN, NaN until 63 observations) and read as a daily cross-sectional percentile rank; ZSCORE of that rank splits the universe into low- and high-liquidity halves at the median. This two-branch split is the compact realization of the tercile grouping: a three-branch tercile tree over the full 63-day dollar-volume rank exceeds the 250-symbol cap, and this median split is exactly the grouping construction on which the size-confound repair was measured in the parent lineage (size correlation cut from +0.24 to +0.1235, noise t +0.59 turned into a stable signal). Within each liquidity half, L=LOG($close+1e-8) is demeaned by its own-group mean, computed as 2*MEAN(indicator*L): MEAN(1[group]*L) is the group sum over the N-name cross-section and each median half holds about N/2 names, so twice it is the group mean. The within-group deviation is then read as a daily cross-sectional percentile rank (outer RANK). Mechanism: 100-share board lots and retail anchoring to the quoted price scale crowd capital-constrained investors into low-priced names inside each liquidity peer group, leaving high-priced peers underpriced, so a HIGH within-group price level predicts HIGHER forward returns over the next 1-20 trading days (positive expected RankIC); the level moves slowly, so turnover stays near zero and the premium decays slowly. Parent 1's dead, library-duplicative momentum premise is deliberately dropped and no opposite-sign blending is used. Hyperparameters: 63-day dollar-volume lookback; median (Z=0) group boundary; structural group-mean multiplier 2 (=N/N_g for a half-universe group, not tuned); 1e-8 log guard; no other windows, thresholds or coefficients; no returns or momentum terms. import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':

The within-group deviation is then read as a daily cross-sectional percentile rank (outer RANK). Hyperparameters: 63-day dollar-volume lookback; median (Z=0) group boundary; structural group-mean multiplier 2 (=N/N_g for a half-universe group, not tuned); 1e-8 log guard; no other windows, thresholds or coefficients; no returns or momentum terms. import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "TS_MEAN(ABS($return - TS_MEAN($return, 20)) * ($volume / (TS_MEAN($volume, 60) + 1e-8)), 20)" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "Vol_Weighted_Return_Dispersion_20D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)

                Concise Observation: Previous factors measuring mean-reversion without removing linear drift have been tested, but isolating the cyclical component after removing the linear trend slope provides an orthogonal measure of overextension.
                Concise Justification: A positive residual from a 20-day linear trend regression normalized by price indicates the stock is trading above its fitted trend line. In a retail-dominated market, such sentiment-driven deviations are temporary and revert, meaning a high residual predicts lower forward returns.
                Concise Knowledge: If a market is retail-dominated with T+1 settlement, sentiment-driven deviations from a fundamental trend are temporary and revert as the trend reasserts; When a stock's price is above its linear trend line, it indicates overextension that will correct.
                concise Specification: Compute REGRESI($close, SEQUENCE(20), 20) / ($close + 1e-8) as the factor. The scope is the daily price data, with a 20-day lookback window. A high factor value (positive residual) is expected to predict lower forward returns over 5-10 days.
                Expected IC Sign: negative

parent_factors.name: Trend_Residual_VolScaled_20D
parent_factors.description: This factor refines the parent trend-residual signal by normalizing the 20-day linear regression residual with the 20-day rolling standard deviation of the close price instead of the raw price. Normalizing by volatility rather than price scales the overextension relative to the stock's typical recent fluctuations, which aims to improve the magnitude and robustness of the decile spread (net ARR) while reducing correlation with raw short-term price reversal factors.
